newsitem.title: GERMANY: Scientology leader launches new attack on Germany.
newsitem.headline: Scientology leader launches new attack on Germany.

text.p: The president of the U.S.-based Church of Scientology launched a fresh attack on the German government on Thursday after the city of Stuttgart implemented measures to limit the organisation's influence.

In a statement released in Los Angeles, Heber Jentzsch accused German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel of inciting a wave of discrimination against the group, and challenged him to debate the issue in public.

In the latest of a number of attacks on Germany, Jentzsch said Kinkel "continues to use the big lie that no discrimination exists... With each new falsehood, he dredges up another petty gauleiter who emerges to perpetrate further oppression against our parishioners".

Germany does not recognise Scientology as a religion, and regional authorities in the southern states of Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg, of which Stuttgart is the capital, have acted to limit its influence in public administration.

Stuttgart's city government said on Wednesday all applicants for jobs in the city's public service would have to give a written assurance that they were not active members of the group. Bavaria's state government has taken similar measures.
Jentzsch branded Stuttgart's move a "reenactment of Hitler's April 1933 law barring non-Aryans from the civil service".

The U.S. State Department's annual human rights report listed Scientology allegations of persecution in Germany, where Scientology says it has around 30,000 members, and the matter was raised briefly on Monday in talks between Kinkel and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Albright said the issue could be handled amicably in bilateral relations, and said Scientology's comparisons with Nazi persecution of the Jews were distasteful.
Kinkel told reporters Scientologists were not persecuted in Germany, and that Germany considered Scientology a profit-making organisation, not a religion.
Several leading German officials say Scientology exploits its members to make profits from expensive self-improvement courses, and say it may be a threat to democracy.

Jentzsch said Kinkel's "venomous diplomacy leads directly to Scientologists losing their jobs, being forbidden to open bank accounts, being denied admission to social groups and having their children harassed at school, if they are even permitted to attend".
